ideas.title: Your Sales Dashboard Is a Drawer of Balls
ideas.era: United States, circa 1890; broad catalog range 1865-1915
ideas.premise: What if today Rex replaced the sales dashboard with a Simplex cash register that counts sales using ceramic balls?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Sales Dashboard Is a Drawer of Balls history

rationale.curiosity: The physical reveal of a dashboard full of balls gives the curiosity gap a precise object.
rationale.cast_comedy: A dropped or misplaced fictional ball can trigger escalating office confusion without inventing historical failure rates.
rationale.modern_contrast: Spreadsheet reporting contrasts directly with a surviving mechanical counting object.
rationale.primary_sources: The Henry Ford provides object 80.33.1 and an institutional explanation of the counting method; catalog dating remains broad.

cast_gags.crow: Raven files the most literal attempt to make sales figures tangible.
cast_gags.pip: Pip carefully registers one imaginary sale with a ball.
cast_gags.mia: Mia separates the sales-count drawer from the money drawer.
cast_gags.rex: Rex asks for a live dashboard and is handed a very heavy drawer.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy rolls one loose prop across the meeting table while everyone watches.

ideas.title: Your Office Kitchen Needs an 1886 Patent
ideas.premise: What if today the office tried to solve its dirty-cup feud with the dishwashing machine in Josephine Cochran's 1886 patent?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Office Kitchen Needs an 1886 Patent history

rationale.curiosity: A familiar office argument opens onto a real patent, with a concrete reveal rather than an invention superlative.
rationale.cast_comedy: The cast can turn a passive-aggressive cup dispute into a causal attempt to build a solution.
rationale.modern_contrast: Shared-kitchen etiquette contrasts directly with a documented nineteenth-century machine.
rationale.primary_sources: A museum-hosted patent drawing has a patent number and grant date; detailed operation still needs the full specification.

cast_gags.crow: Raven opens a folder on the least glamorous office arms race.
cast_gags.pip: Pip tries to identify his mug beneath a mountain of unwashed cups.
cast_gags.mia: Mia replaces Rex's motivational dishwashing memo with a patent drawing.
cast_gags.rex: Rex markets the machine as an employee-engagement initiative while avoiding the sink.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy adds one final spoon just as the demonstration is declared finished.

sources.institution: National Women's History Museum via Google Arts & Culture
sources.locator: Josephine Cochran Patent US355139-0; patent 355,139; grant 28 December 1886; metadata creation 31 December 1885

ideas.title: The Office Snack Machine Runs on Elbow Grease
ideas.era: Western India, early twentieth century, catalog date 1901-1930
ideas.premise: What if today the office snack break required Pip to turn a wheel-and-rope butter churner before anybody could claim the butter?
ideas.benchmark_query: The Office Snack Machine Runs on Elbow Grease history

rationale.curiosity: A hand-powered snack break has a clear physical reveal without a fake productivity claim.
rationale.cast_comedy: The cast can build one escalating queue around a real mechanism, aiming jokes at office management.
rationale.modern_contrast: Push-button convenience contrasts with a cataloged hand-operated churner.
rationale.primary_sources: Sanskriti Museums identifies a specific object, place, date range, and materials; prevalence and output are not established.

cast_gags.crow: Raven introduces a fictional wellness policy that accidentally makes sense only to Rex.
cast_gags.pip: Pip turns the wheel while his break clock keeps running.
cast_gags.mia: Mia demonstrates why the rope transfers motion rather than generating free labor.
cast_gags.rex: Rex calls the queue a team-building success before helping himself.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy attaches an imaginary number dispenser and instantly becomes queue manager.

ideas.title: Your Spare Change Has Jury Duty
ideas.era: England, documented from at least 1282; surviving standards from 1477
ideas.premise: What if today your spare change had to face an independent jury before Rex would accept it at the office coffee counter?
ideas.benchmark_query: Your Spare Change Has Jury Duty history

rationale.curiosity: The reversal puts coins on trial and immediately promises an explainable historical mechanism.
rationale.cast_comedy: Rex can obstruct a tiny purchase until Mia distinguishes inspection from theatrical prosecution.
rationale.modern_contrast: Routine contactless convenience contrasts with sampling and physical coin tests.
rationale.primary_sources: Royal Mint Museum interpretation and a collection overview are located; no original medieval proceeding has been inspected.

cast_gags.crow: Raven announces that the defendant is a coin, not its owner.
cast_gags.pip: Pip arrives with exact change and discovers a ceremonial waiting room.
cast_gags.mia: Mia brings scales to stop Rex judging the coin by its expression.
cast_gags.rex: Rex wears a comically oversized robe to supervise one imaginary coffee purchase.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy volunteers a chocolate coin; Mia removes it before any real test.

sources.locator: Trial of the Pyx; opening paragraph and explanation of jury tests
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

sources.locator: Trial Plates collection overview; standards described as dating from 1477
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: The coffee-counter tribunal is invented. The museum describes independent checking since at least 1282 and later surviving standards; neither establishes that every historical customer had coins individually approved. Collection overview is not a transcript of a medieval trial.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Locate an original trial record and period-specific sampling rules before narrating medieval procedure, penalties, or uninterrupted annual operation.

ideas.title: IT Support Wants the Actual Bug
ideas.premise: What if today IT refused to close Pip's ticket until he attached the actual physical bug, inspired by the moth preserved in a 1947 computer logbook?
ideas.benchmark_query: IT Support Wants the Actual Bug history

rationale.curiosity: A literal attachment rule provides an immediate physical payoff for a familiar software phrase.
rationale.cast_comedy: The team can escalate a support ticket without turning a disputed origin myth into a fact.
rationale.modern_contrast: An online attachment workflow becomes a tangible museum-record problem.
rationale.primary_sources: Smithsonian identifies the actual logbook and accession; local retrieval and wording must still pass the anchor check.

cast_gags.crow: Raven distinguishes a real insect record from the myth that it invented the word bug.
cast_gags.pip: Pip dutifully uploads a screenshot and receives an imaginary request for a specimen.
cast_gags.mia: Mia points to the institutional record instead of crediting one celebrity with everything.
cast_gags.rex: Rex expands the attachment field into a ridiculous oversized evidence tray.
cast_gags.timmy: Timmy submits a paper moth that Mia labels fictional before the punchline.

sources.institution: Smithsonian Institution / National Museum of American History
sources.locator: Log Book With Computer Bug; nmah_334663; ID 1994.0191.01; 1947
sources.verification_scope: Official source and stated anchors, not automatic semantic entailment

ideas.fact_boundary: Smithsonian describes a moth preserved by the Mark II team and explicitly says engineering bugs predate it. Do not claim Hopper found it personally, owned this book, coined bug, or established the first software error. The modern support rule is fictional.
research_questions: [VERIFICAR] Confirm the original page date and wording from a legible reproduction before quoting it; do not substitute the ENIAC-looking URL slug for the record's Mark II description.
